chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Abdullah ibn Sinan who said:

I mentioned to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) a man afflicted with obsessive doubts regarding wudu and salat, and I said, 'He is an intelligent man.' So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said: 'And what intellect does he have, while he is obeying Shaytan?' So I said to him, 'And how is he obeying Shaytan?' So he said: 'Ask him about this that comes to him — from which thing is it? For he will tell you: it is from the acts of Shaytan.'

key_terms.عَاقِلٌ: rational/intelligent — the narrator's assumption is subverted by the Imam
key_terms.مُبْتَلًى: afflicted/obsessed — used for someone seized by a persistent condition, here the compulsive repetition of wudu and salat
key_terms.وَسْوَاس: waswas — obsessive doubt or whispering, understood here though not explicitly stated
key_terms.يُطِيعُ الشَّيْطَانَ: obeying Shaytan — the Imam's shocking reframe of the man's apparent piety

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq say about a person obsessed with repeating wudu and salat?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) identifies obsessive compulsive doubt (waswas) in acts of worship as a form of obedience to Shaytan, not a sign of piety or intelligence. The hadith reflects the classical Shia legal and ethical position that excessive doubt in ritual purity and prayer is spiritually harmful, not virtuous. Early Muslim scholars recognized waswas as a distinct psychological-spiritual affliction, and this hadith's rhetorical strategy — instructing the narrator to ask the afflicted person about the origin of his doubt — exposes that the person himself would admit its satanic source.
